_**A New Old Play**_ (Chinese: 椒麻堂會) is a 2021 [epic film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_film "Epic film") directed and written by [Qiu Jiongjiong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qiu_Jiongjiong "Qiu Jiongjiong"). As Qiu's seventh film, it marks his first [fictional feature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narrative_film "Narrative film"). A co-production between Hong Kong's Uluka Productions and France's Hippocampe Productions, the film stars Yi Sicheng as Qiu Fu, a recently deceased [Sichuan opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sichuan_opera "Sichuan opera") actor, alongside Guan Nan, Qiu Zhimin, Gu Tao, and Xue Xuchun. The story chronicles Qiu Fu's life and career in [China from the 1920s to the 1980s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_China#Modern_China "History of China") through his remembrances during his journey into the [netherworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youdu "Youdu"), featuring events such as the [Second Sino-Japanese War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Sino-Japanese_War "Second Sino-Japanese War"), the [Chinese Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Civil_War "Chinese Civil War"), the [Great Chinese Famine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chinese_Famine "Great Chinese Famine"), and the [Cultural Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution").

Qiu Jiongjiong conceived of the project in 2017 after illustrating the [biography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biography "Biography") for his grandfather and Sichuan opera actor Qiu Fu. Inspired to tell the story with film, Qiu based the protagonist on his grandfather and began developing a screenplay from May 2017 to February 2018 under the [working title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_title "Working title") _The Neo-New Adventures_. Production design spanned six months before [principal photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") began in August 2019 in [Leshan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leshan "Leshan"), [Sichuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sichuan "Sichuan") over three months. Post-production took place in France, with French filmmaker [Marie-Pierre Duhamel-Muller](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marie-Pierre_Duhamel-Muller&action=edit&redlink=1 "Marie-Pierre Duhamel-Muller (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie-Pierre_Duhamel-Muller "fr:Marie-Pierre Duhamel-Muller")) involved in the editing. The film also marks the second film to be primarily in [Sichuanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sichuanese_dialects "Sichuanese dialects"), after the 1962 film _Conscription_.

_A New Old Play_ had its world premiere in competition for the [Golden Leopard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Leopard "Golden Leopard") at the [74th Locarno Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/74th_Locarno_Film_Festival "74th Locarno Film Festival") on 13 August 2021, where it received the [Special Jury Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Jury_Prize_/(Locarno_International_Film_Festival/) "Special Jury Prize (Locarno International Film Festival)"). It also garnered various accolades and received positive reviews from critics, with praises particularly on its themes, narrative style and complexities, and production design. Due to [censorship in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_censorship_in_China "Film censorship in China"), only single-time private screenings were held worldwide from 2021 to 2022. The film received its first [wide release](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wide_release "Wide release") in France on 30 April 2025.

Qiu Fu, a renowned [Sichuan opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sichuan_opera "Sichuan opera") actor, meets his demise. [Ox-Head and Horse-Face](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ox-Head_and_Horse-Face "Ox-Head and Horse-Face") are sent to escort him into the [netherworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youdu "Youdu") to perform for [Yanluo Wang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yanluo_Wang "Yanluo Wang"). Qiu refuses to accept his fate and tries to flee, much to the envoys' confusion as they ask him how he, who has been an artiste since the age of eight, does not embrace death. Qiu retorts that he began his opera journey at seven and starts to reminisce about his life.

During the [Warlord Era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warlord_Era "Warlord Era"), an operaphile Pocky rises through the ranks to become a military commander. He uses his newfound power to form an opera troupe called the New-New Theatre School. Early in its operation, Qiu Fu, a foundling of a famous opera actor who died performing on stage, is sent to the troupe by his mother, who abandons him to remarry. Qiu learns opera singing from the troupe's teachers, but his performances are unsatisfactory. One day, while practising, he encounters Pocky, who takes a liking to him and accepts him as an apprentice. After some training, Qiu debuts as an opera performer. The [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") soon breaks out, and the troupe begins charity tours to raise funds against [Japan's invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Sino-Japanese_War "Second Sino-Japanese War"). One night, Qiu is intoxicated after drinking a bowl of poisonous mushroom soup and dreams of flying across the city on a leaf, only to be bombed by a Japanese fighter jet.

In the netherworld, Qiu follows the envoys to the [Naihe Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-existence#Chinese_mythology "Pre-existence"), where he encounters Crooky, a servant of the troupe who mysteriously disappeared decades ago. The envoys explain that they never received orders to take Crooky, but he keeps returning to the netherworld, trapping his soul between realms. He opens an inn at the Naihe Bridge to welcome both the deceased and [demons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaoguai "Yaoguai"). Qiu decides to reunite with Crooky and stays at the inn while watching his young apprentices perform [rituals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_funeral_rituals "Chinese funeral rituals") in the living world. Dissatisfied with their performances, he reminisces about his own early career.

By 1945, Qiu has established himself as an opera actor. However, Pocky, now a [warlord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warlord "Warlord"), worries about his fate under [Chiang Kai-shek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiang_Kai-shek "Chiang Kai-shek")'s rule and loses interest in opera. Before [the Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Civil_War#Immediate_post-war_clashes_\(1945%E2%80%931946\) "Chinese Civil War"), he disbands the troupe to protect the actors and their families from his impending downfall. Unemployed, Qiu's life worsens even after the establishment of the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China"), when the troupe is reformed and renamed the People's Sichuan Opera Troupe. Qiu's daughter dies subsequently during the [Great Chinese Famine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chinese_Famine "Great Chinese Famine"), but his son Hei survives. One day, Qiu finds [an abandoned infant girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Female_infanticide_in_China "Female infanticide in China") on the street and, despite his meager living conditions, takes her in. He and his wife struggle to feed her and resort to stealing [feces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_feces "Human feces"), only to be caught by [cadres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadre_system_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "Cadre system of the Chinese Communist Party") who accuse them of stealing [state property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_property "Public property"). Qiu sings to the cadres, leveraging his fame as an actor to escape. They manage to cook the [maggots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maggots "Maggots") found in the feces to feed the girl, sustaining her life. Later, the girl's mother returns, claiming she abandoned her only because her husband tried to eat the child. Though reluctant, Qiu's wife returns the baby. During the [Cultural Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution"), the New-New troupe is [labeled as feudal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution#Opera_and_music "Cultural Revolution"), [facing persecution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Struggle_session "Struggle session") from the [Red Guards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Guards "Red Guards"). Hei, now a teenager, wishes to join the [Big Link-up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Exchange_of_Revolutionary_Experience "Great Exchange of Revolutionary Experience") in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing") but is locked up by his family. Desperate, he escapes through a window and flies across the city on a leaf. Years later, now a high-ranking Red Guard, Hei returns home and learns that Qiu is released from [labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-education_through_labor "Re-education through labor") and assigned to minor roles in plays.

After reminiscing about his career, Qiu bids farewell to Crooky and shares one last drink with the envoys. Confused about how he will remember all his lines after drinking the [Meng-po soup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meng_Po "Meng Po"), he is reassured by the envoys that his artistic intuition will guide him. Qiu boards the boat and reaches the other side, queuing for the Meng-po soup before drinking it all. The [camera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movie_camera "Movie camera") pans to each of the other characters drinking the soup at various moments, then returns to Qiu's empty seat. [The director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qiu_Jiongjiong "Qiu Jiongjiong"), in modern attire, sits down and is served a bowl of Meng-po soup.

*   Yi Sicheng as Qiu Fu, a renowned Sichuan opera actor of the New-New Theatre School[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-NYTReview-1)
    *   Chen Haoyu as young Qiu Fu, a seven-year-old foundling who becomes an opera student[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-NewYorkerReview-2)
*   Guan Nan as Tong Huafeng, Qiu's wife[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-NYTReview-1)
*   Qiu Zhimin as Pocky, a military commander, opera enthusiast, and the founder of the New-New Theatre School[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-NewYorkerReview-2)
*   Gu Tao as Crooky, a servant at the New-New Theatre School who eventually becomes an inn owner in the netherworld[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-PArticlesMarch2023-3)
*   Xue Xuchun as:
    *   Ah Hei, Qiu's son[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4)
    *   Chicken Foot,[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-5) a cook at Pocky's inn[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-CinemaScopeSeptember2022-6)

In addition, Liu Boyu and Huang Lingchao appear as [Ox-Head and Horse-Face](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ox-Head_and_Horse-Face "Ox-Head and Horse-Face"), the envoys of the netherworld,[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-7) while director [Qiu Jiongjiong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qiu_Jiongjiong "Qiu Jiongjiong") made a cameo appearance as himself.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-BerryVoiceover-8): 294

> "I began to piece together the story of an ordinary man, a man who embodied the spirit of a clown, living through the greatest upheavals of our times. There is nothing new under the sun, as we know. However, these characters are just like you and me, and we each in our own way will continue to repeat this same song of humanity."

—Qiu Jiongjiong, the director and writer, on the inspiration behind the screenplay for _A New Old Play_[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9)

Qiu Fu, the grandfather of director [Qiu Jiongjiong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qiu_Jiongjiong "Qiu Jiongjiong"), was a [Sichuan opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sichuan_opera "Sichuan opera") actor who gained fame for playing [_chou_ roles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chou_role "Chou role")[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-10) in the 1930s and 1940s throughout [Sichuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sichuan "Sichuan").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) He died in 1987 when Qiu Jiongjiong was ten years old.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-BerryVoiceover-8): 293  Growing up in [Leshan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leshan "Leshan"), Sichuan, Qiu Jiongjiong developed an interest in Sichuan opera influenced by his grandfather, which ultimately inspired him to pursue a career in filmmaking.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-CinemaScopeSeptember2022-6) He also described having a "close" relationship with his grandfather, who served as a "crucial figure in \[his\] artistic inspirations" for his artworks and films.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) After making the documentary film _[Mr. Zhang Believes](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mr._Zhang_Believes&action=edit&redlink=1 "Mr. Zhang Believes (page does not exist)") ([zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%99%A1_/(2014%E5%B9%B4%E7%B4%80%E9%8C%84%E7%89%87/) "zh:癡 (2014年紀錄片)"))_ (2015), Qiu struggled with inspiration for several years despite still wanting to create films.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-CinemaScopeSeptember2022-6) In 2017, on the 30th anniversary of Qiu Fu's death, Qiu Jiongjiong's father began writing a [biography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biography "Biography") to commemorate Qiu Fu and asked Qiu to illustrate for the book.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-MirrorMedia009-11) After creating illustrations for all 15 chapters in two months, Qiu felt a sense of "incompleteness" and wanted to approach the subject of his grandfather "through the medium of film", which inspired him to start writing the screenplay that would become _A New Old Play_.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-MirrorMedia009-11) It marks the second film produced by Qiu Jiongjiong featuring Qiu Fu, following the documentary short film _Ode to Joy_ (2007), which depicted a stage performance in remembrance of the 20th anniversary of Qiu Fu's death and was cited by Qiu as a significant inspiration for _A New Old Play_'s focus on the lives of ordinary people.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-CinemaScopeSeptember2022-6)

Qiu Jiongjiong began writing the screenplay in May 2017 and completed it in February 2018, taking about seven months to finish a script that exceeded 100,000 words.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-BerryVoiceover-8): 293  He based the story on his father's biography, along with some additional background research.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) It marks Qiu's seventh film and first [fictional feature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narrative_film "Narrative film").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-CNAJune2022-12)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-13) Qiu described the story itself as "[non-fictional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-fictional "Non-fictional")", and he only aimed to create a sense of fiction through the film's aesthetics, drawing inspiration from both Chinese and Western stage plays.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-BerryVoiceover-8): 289  The screenplay emphasises Qiu Fu's status as a _chou_, which Qiu Jiongjiong referred to as the "clown spirit", calling it the "core and quintessence of his cinematic grammar".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-CinemaScopeSeptember2022-6) He cited [Federico Fellini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Fellini "Federico Fellini")'s works as an inspiration, highlighting how [circus clowns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circus_clown "Circus clown") served as [viewpoint characters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viewpoint_character "Viewpoint character") in his films.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-BerryVoiceover-8): 288  In Sichuan opera, _chou_ roles (clowns) are usually not essential to the storyline but serve as the focal point, which Qiu referred to as the "author's perspective".[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) In addition to Qiu Fu, Qiu Jiongjiong also created other clown-like characters, such as Crooky and Chicken Foot.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4) These characters exist beyond the chronological timeline and the boundaries of the living and the dead in the plot, allowing them to serve as [narrators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narrator "Narrator") and [storytellers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storytelling "Storytelling").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4) He utilised these characters to interject the narrative to create a [distancing effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distancing_effect "Distancing effect"),[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-14) but rather than directly [breaking the fourth wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breaking_the_fourth_wall "Breaking the fourth wall"), Qiu aimed to re-examine the story naturally from the narrator and storyteller's perspectives.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9)

Qiu drew inspiration from his personal experiences and [Sichuanese culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sichuanese_culture "Sichuanese culture") for the portrayal of clowns, noting that [Sichuanese people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sichuanese_people "Sichuanese people") are known for their optimism and [dark sense of humour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_humor "Dark humor") despite facing fate and suffering, qualities he found resonant with clowns' modest demeanor and playful exterior.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-CinemaScopeSeptember2022-6) Qiu also referenced the [Great Chinese Famine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chinese_Famine "Great Chinese Famine") in the film, a topic often omitted in other [epic films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_film "Epic film") like _[Farewell My Concubine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farewell_My_Concubine_/(film/) "Farewell My Concubine (film)")_ and _[The Blue Kite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blue_Kite "The Blue Kite")_ (both 1993), explaining that he included it because he based the story primarily on his grandfather's biography and aimed to restore the original narrative.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4) However, he noted that there are limited records about his grandfather's life during the [Cultural Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution"), and he had interviewed an elderly person knowledgeable about his grandfather's adoption of an infant girl for additional information.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4) He concluded the screenplay with an [anticlimax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anticlimax_/(narrative/) "Anticlimax (narrative)") to reflect the daily lives of ordinary people, noting that while their stories may lack a [climactic arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_arc "Character arc"), they can still convey profound emotional depth.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-BerryVoiceover-8): 296  The project was showcased at the [Golden Horse Project Promotion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Horse_Film_Festival_and_Awards "Golden Horse Film Festival and Awards") in November 2017, where it won the CNC Prize from the [Centre national du cinéma et de l'image animée](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_national_du_cin%C3%A9ma_et_de_l%27image_anim%C3%A9e "Centre national du cinéma et de l'image animée").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-15) In May 2018, it received the Hubert Bals Fund at the [International Film Festival Rotterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Film_Festival_Rotterdam "International Film Festival Rotterdam"), under the [working title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_title "Working title") _The Neo-New Adventures_,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-16)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-17)[\[c\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-18) named after the opera troupe established at the film's opening.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-CinemaScopeSeptember2022-6) The first [table-read](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table-read "Table-read") took place in the same month, and the cast was given a year to prepare for their characters.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-MirrorMedia008-19)

Most of the actors and crew members are Qiu's family and friends, with many crew members also appeared in minor roles in the film.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-PArticlesMarch2023-3)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) He cast them because he wanted to tell the story "locally", and described the shoot as a "party" among his closed ones.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) Yi Sicheng, a film festival curator who befriended Qiu at the YunFest Film Festival and made a brief appearance in _Mr. Zhang Believes_, was invited by Qiu to star in the lead role.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-MirrorMedia008-19) Qiu chose to avoid casting an actor of a similar age to the character Qiu Fu, as he felt the demeanor of actors around the same age as the character was unsuitable, and he was drawn to Yi's "old-timer" vibes, which he described as both "elegant and resilient".[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-MirrorMedia008-19) Guan Nan (who portrayed Tong Huafeng) and Xue Xuchan (who played dual roles as Hei and Chicken Foot) were also both film festival curators.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4) Qiu chose Xue for the role of Chicken Foot due to his comedic awareness, and Xue received dialect coaching to prepare for his characters, as Hei speaks in [Southwestern Mandarin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwestern_Mandarin "Southwestern Mandarin") while Chicken Foot uses the [Leshan dialect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leshan_dialect "Leshan dialect") with an [Emei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emeishan_City "Emeishan City") accent.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4) Qu Tao, an independent documentary filmmaker, was cast as the [aphasic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphasia "Aphasia") character Crooky, specifically designed by Qiu because he believed Qu would struggle to remember the character's lines.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-PArticlesMarch2023-3) Qiu Zhimin and Chen Haoyu, who played Pocky and young Qiu Fu, are Qiu Jiongjiong's father and nephew, respectively.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) Despite initially hesitating to cast his father due to his age, Qiu Jiongjiong ultimately agreed when his father volunteered for the role, noting his similarities to Pocky.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-InitiumMediaApril2023-20) Qiu's cousin composed the film's score,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-PArticlesMarch2023-3) drawing on elements from Sichuan opera,[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) while his uncle served as the artistic advisor.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) Qiu Jiongjiong made a cameo appearance at the end of the film, citing his reasons as being both the author and part of the [family history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_history "Family history") central to the story, as well as his desire to become part of the history of clowns as both a descendant and an enthusiast.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-BerryVoiceover-8): 294  All actors, except for the troupe teachers, were untrained, while the troupe roles were filled by professional Sichuan opera actors.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9)

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/e/ed/ANewOldPlayBoatScene.png/250px-ANewOldPlayBoatScene.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ANewOldPlayBoatScene.png)

The film utilised visibly fake backdrops and set design, such as white fabrics to mimic turbulent waves during the disbandment scene of the New-New Theatre School, a style reminiscent of stage plays

Set construction spanned about six months.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4) The shoot took place entirely at a factory owned by a friend of Qiu's, with the production set constructed in a [textile mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Textile_mill "Textile mill") covering approximately 400 square meters (~4,306 square feet).[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-PArticlesMarch2023-3) A white shed was also built in the factory's parking lot, bringing the total size of the sets to about 1,000 square meters (~10,764 square feet).[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) It was also the filming location for Qiu's previous film _Mr. Zhang Believes_, for which he wrote the screenplay with that set in mind.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-BerryVoiceover-8): 293  He likened the production style to the works of [Italo Calvino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italo_Calvino "Italo Calvino"),[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-MirrorMedia006-21) and explained that he chose a similar set design with _Mr. Zhang Believes_ because he saw handcrafted production design as "an extension of creative invention", aiming to "refurbish through techniques" from early screen and stage plays.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) Qiu Jiongjiong (who was a trained visual artist) served as the art director and participated in creating the set props.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-MirrorMedia006-21)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-PArticlesMarch2023-3) The set was mainly decorated with hand-painted artwork,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-PArticlesMarch2023-3) while all the props, walls, staircases, and backdrops were also hand-crafted.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) Most materials used for the set renovations were sourced directly from the surrounding factory, primarily utilising cloth, along with cardboard, wood, and cotton.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-PArticlesMarch2023-3)

Qiu emphasised that he chose to use "exaggerated" set and props to suit the film's tone of absurdity and [black humour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_humour "Black humour").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-BerryVoiceover-8): 289  He also created and manipulated a "sense of alienation" through low-budget filmmaking, using visibly fake backgrounds and a theatrical style of production sets, influenced by [Bertolt Brecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertolt_Brecht "Bertolt Brecht")'s plays.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-CinemaScopeSeptember2022-6) For instance, a grey cloth was used to represent a river,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-PArticlesMarch2023-3) while wind-blown plastic bags and shaking white fabrics were used to mimic the turbulent waves,[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-34SMFebruary2023-22)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-LianheZaobaoReview-23) with critics comparing the scantily decorated settings to [Roy Andersson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Andersson "Roy Andersson")'s films.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-PArticlesMarch2023-3)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ChinaFilmNewsReview-24) Lin Sheng-wei at _[United Daily News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Daily_News "United Daily News")_ compared the "flimsy" and simplistic scenery to [stage plays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stage_play "Stage play"), calling it a "forced [defamiliarization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defamiliarization "Defamiliarization")" that required the audience to "use their imagination in every scene", which encourages the audience to focus on the characters and immerse in their emotions to "make the absurd props come to life";[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-25) while _[34th Street Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/34th_Street_Magazine "34th Street Magazine")_'s Weike Li described the "obviously contrived sets" as "intentionally creating a sense of comical foreignness", presenting history in [expressionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expressionism "Expressionism").[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-34SMFebruary2023-22) While designing the [netherworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youdu "Youdu"), Qiu cited [Jacques Tati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Tati "Jacques Tati")'s visual style as an inspiration, and made limited distinctions from the living world sets, primarily by dimming the [lighting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_lighting "Film lighting") and using black-coloured props instead of white.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-InitiumMediaApril2023-20)

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Leshan_%2816989556077%29.jpg/250px-Leshan_%2816989556077%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leshan_/(16989556077/).jpg)

Filming took place at Qiu Jiongjiong's hometown [Leshan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leshan "Leshan")

[Principal photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") began in August 2019 in Leshan, Sichuan, China,[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-MirrorMedia008-19)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-PArticlesTing-26) the hometown of Qiu Jiongjiong.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-CinemaScopeSeptember2022-6) Filming lasted a total of 83 days over a three-month period.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) Robbin Feng served as the cinematographer,[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-27) using an [Arri Alexa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arri_Alexa "Arri Alexa") for the shoot, a camera model that Qiu described as "better than anything \[he had\] worked with before".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-CinemaScopeSeptember2022-6) In terms of cinematography, [horizontal shifts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracking_shot "Tracking shot") and [lateral camera movements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panning_/(camera/) "Panning (camera)") were primarily employed to present the composition as an "unveiling scroll of [Chinese painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_painting "Chinese painting")".[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-MirrorMedia006-21) The composition was mainly planimetric, with the camera positioned at a 90-degree angle to the actors and utilising perpendicular [tracking shots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracking_shot "Tracking shot").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-CinemaScopeSeptember2022-6) Qiu aimed to convey a sense of [epic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_poetry "Epic poetry") scale by emphasising the shallow depth of field in the set design,[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-MirrorMedia006-21) and compared the composition to the [triptychs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triptych "Triptych") and [frescoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frescoes "Frescoes") of [Giotto di Bondone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giotto_di_Bondone "Giotto di Bondone").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) The production team planned the shooting schedule in advance, allowing set pieces to be disassembled and reassembled between scenes.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) The costumes used in the film were all from Qiu Jiongjiong's father's former opera troupe.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4)

The entire cast stayed in Leshan for a month after filming to record their dialogues,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4) as no sounds were [recorded on location](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_recording_and_reproduction "Sound recording and reproduction") during filming.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-MirrorMedia006-21)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-PArticlesMarch2023-3) Qiu cited several reasons for this decision, including to avoid the high costs of on-site recording, the background noises at the factory, and the fact that most of the actors were non-locals who could not speak in standard Leshan dialects, therefore he decided to record dialogue after the filming wrapped.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-PArticlesMarch2023-3) He also noted that it could enable the dialects to be delivered more precisely, allowing actors to adjust their emotions for a better performance, while [crowd scenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crowd_scene "Crowd scene") and scenes without visible lip movements also permit changes to the dialogue.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4) He chose to feature the film's dialogues in [Sichuanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sichuanese_dialects "Sichuanese dialects"), his native language, which he described as "vivid and humorous" and having a "strong nostalgia" stemming from the dialect's evolution over hundreds of years since [the diaspora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sichuanese_people "Sichuanese people") from other [provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_China "Provinces of China") during the [Ming Dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_Dynasty "Ming Dynasty").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) This film is the second to be made primarily in Sichuanese since _Conscription_ (1962).[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) [Dubbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubbing "Dubbing") was supervised by [sound designer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_designer "Sound designer") Wang Ran, who also created all the sound effects for the film.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4)

Post-production took place in France,[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-MirrorMedia006-21) with Qiu also serving as the editor.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-28) French filmmaker [Marie-Pierre Duhamel-Muller](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marie-Pierre_Duhamel-Muller&action=edit&redlink=1 "Marie-Pierre Duhamel-Muller (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie-Pierre_Duhamel-Muller "fr:Marie-Pierre Duhamel-Muller")), who edited _Mr. Zhang Believes_, was also involved in the editing through [video conferences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_conference "Video conference") and provided advice on restructuring the narrative.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-MirrorMedia006-21) The film features two parallel narratives, one set in the living world and the other in the netherworld, with both timelines unfolding [linearly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_narrative "Linear narrative") and the living world timeline is interspersed into the netherworld timeline as [flashbacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flashback_/(narrative/) "Flashback (narrative)").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-BerryVoiceover-8): 293–294  Producer Ding Ningyuan described the post-production process as "tense" due to budget constraints and the need to meet deadlines for film festivals.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4) The film is co-produced by Hong Kong's Uluka Productions and France's Hippocampe Productions.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ScreenDailyJuly2021-29) Parallax, the rights division of Midnight Blur Films, managed its international sales.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-VarietyNovember2021-30)

The film was presented at the [Hong Kong-Asia Film Financing Forum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Expo_Hong_Kong "Entertainment Expo Hong Kong") in June 2020,[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-31) and at [Marché du Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March%C3%A9_du_Film "Marché du Film") in July 2021, where it was retitled _A New Old Play_.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ScreenDailyJuly2021-29) Regarding the film titles, Qiu named the film _Jiaoma tanghui_ ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_characters "Traditional Chinese characters"): 椒麻堂會) in Chinese.[\[d\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-32) He literally translated the Chinese title to "The Gathering and Celebration of Peppery and Chili Flavors",[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) which reflects the main character Qiu Fu's roots and occupation as a performer both before and after death and he felt it more accurately described the film.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-CinemaScopeSeptember2022-6) The English title, _A New Old Play_, was suggested by the producer and the English subtitles translator, which Qiu found captured the film's themes of "history endlessly repeating itself" and evoking "a sense of [déjà vu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9j%C3%A0_vu "Déjà vu")".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-CinemaScopeSeptember2022-6) In November 2021, the film was also showcased at TIFFCOM, [Tokyo International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_International_Film_Festival "Tokyo International Film Festival")'s project market.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-VarietyNovember2021-30)

### Portrayal of history

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=A_New_Old_Play&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Portrayal of history")\]

_A New Old Play_ chronicles a series of [Chinese historical events from the 1920s to the 1980s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_China#Modern_China "History of China"), including the collapse of the [Qing dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasty "Qing dynasty"), the [Warlord Era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warlord_Era "Warlord Era"), [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") and the [fall of Nanking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing_Massacre "Nanjing Massacre"), the [Chinese Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Civil_War "Chinese Civil War"), [Mao Zedong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_Zedong "Mao Zedong")'s [Communist Party rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party"), the [Great Chinese Famine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chinese_Famine "Great Chinese Famine"), the [Great Leap Forward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Leap_Forward "Great Leap Forward"), and the [Cultural Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution").[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-33) Qiu Jiongjiong identified a theme of the film as the notion that history endlessly repeats itself.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-CinemaScopeSeptember2022-6) He summarised that the film's overall tone conveys the tragedy of destiny, aiming to create a contrast between the vividness of each individual and the cruelty of their irresistible fates.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-BerryVoiceover-8): 292  Qiu also explained that he found many historical narratives focus on context or abstract ideologies, but when the emphasis is placed on particular individuals, it becomes easier to "identify certain problems".[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-34)

Film scholar [Hao Jian](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hao_Jian&action=edit&redlink=1 "Hao Jian (page does not exist)") ([zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%83%9D%E5%BB%BA "zh:郝建")) specifically commented on the film's approach to presenting [historical memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_memory "Historical memory") through familial and personal experiences, which aligns with [Michel Foucault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Foucault "Michel Foucault")'s discourse on popular memory and allows for a "faithful" portrayal of history, but from a new perspective that reinterprets and questions history—specifically, in the case of _A New Old Play_, from the perspective of a clown and infused with a sense of comedy.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-JianMay2024-35): 145–146  Qiu stated that he did not intend to recreate historical scenes but rather aimed to convey a general sense of the historical context of that time through metaphorical expressions, such as the film's simplistic and theatrical production style.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4) Academic Isha Ting noted that the film's aesthetics resonate with Brecht's distancing effect, which encourages the audience to focus on social roots and structures while reflecting on what can be transformed.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-PArticlesTing-26)

> "In this film, the connection between those onstage and offstage, as well as inside and outside the Sichuan opera being put together in the story, is blurred. What happens onstage is integrated into the narrative, and the expressions onstage are blended into the characters' everyday lives. This is because Sichuan opera took root in my body and soul through the mundanity of everyday life. Just like when generations of Sichuan opera goers, who spent much of their time in the theater weeping, sighing, falling asleep, etc., their lives are in a way inter-textualized with the performance on stage, creating an adventitious symmetry of life itself; were they just watching a performance, or are they themselves a part of, or even integrated into the performance?"

—Qiu Jiongjiong on incorporating the characteristics of Sichuan opera into the narrative[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9)

Qiu described his motive for creating _A New Old Play_ as a desire to craft a "Sichuan-flavored saga", incorporating local elements without reducing them to conceptualised spectacles or [stereotypes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereotype "Stereotype").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) Notable elements added to the film include [Sichuanese people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sichuanese_people "Sichuanese people"), [Sichuan opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sichuan_opera "Sichuan opera"), and [Sichuanese dialects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sichuanese_dialects "Sichuanese dialects"), all heavily influenced by the culture surrounding him during his upbringing.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-BeijingYouthDailyJanuary2023-36)

Regarding Sichuan opera, Qiu sought to transform the traditional operatic language into a more accessible form of expression that could effectively communicate while retaining its flavor and melodies, sharing similarities with the works of [Geoffrey Chaucer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Chaucer "Geoffrey Chaucer"), [François Rabelais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Rabelais "François Rabelais"), and [Giovanni Boccaccio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Boccaccio "Giovanni Boccaccio").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) Despite featuring exaggerated theatrical staging in its production design, film scholar [Michael Berry](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_Berry_\(scholar\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Michael Berry (scholar) (page does not exist)") ([zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%99%BD%E7%9D%BF%E6%96%87 "zh:白睿文")) observed that these production values closely parallel Sichuan opera, which enhance the authenticity and emotional depth of the performances while maintaining the overall tone of [realism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Realism_/(arts/) "Realism (arts)").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-BerryVoiceover-8): 292  Qiu identified the characteristics of Sichuan opera as "mundanity of everyday life" filled with expressions of deep and personal humanity, and he integrated these characteristics into the story, blending the ordinary with the daily lives of the characters.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) He compared the viewing experience to that of opera-goers [inter-textualizing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertextuality "Intertextuality") with the stage performances, creating a symmetry with their own lives and immersing themselves in the performance.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-DGenerateMarch2022-9) Scholar [Wong Nim-yan](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wong_Nim-yan&action=edit&redlink=1 "Wong Nim-yan (page does not exist)") ([zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%BB%83%E5%BF%B5%E6%AC%A3 "zh:黃念欣")) also recognised this perspective, noting that there are limited Sichuan opera scenes in the film, but the cinematography, production design, and dialogues strongly resemble it, and compared its central thought to traditional Sichuan opera pieces like _Inn of Successive Promotion_ (連升店) and _Writing Essays_ (做文章), suggesting that the film itself can be viewed as a form of Sichuan opera.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-37)

The film also explores [thanatology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thanatology "Thanatology"), which Qiu describes as stemming from the Sichuanese people's understanding of life and death.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-BerryVoiceover-8): 294  A significant part of the film is set in the [underworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underworld "Underworld"), using a secular perspective to speculate about the [afterlife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afterlife "Afterlife").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-BerryVoiceover-8): 294  He found that the Sichuanese people hold an optimistic view of death, citing traditional _Ba Ba banquets_ (壩壩宴), family banquets held for both weddings and funerals, as an example and describing them as a reflection of the Sichuanese perspective on death as "a harmony between sorrow and joy".[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-BeijingYouthDailyJanuary2023-36) He composed the story in which the protagonist reflects on his life and anticipates his post-death journey, aligning it with Sichuanese views on death and describing the film as "a flowing banquet of life and death".[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ThePaperJanuary2023-4)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-BerryVoiceover-8): 294

_A New Old Play_, like all of Qiu Jiongjiong's previous documentaries, was unable to obtain a [film public screening permit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_public_screening_permit "Film public screening permit") from the [China Film Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Film_Administration "China Film Administration"), which prevented its official release in China and only unauthorised private screenings were held in the country from 2021 to 2022.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-PArticlesTing-26) Une Cinema De Vent, the non-profit organisation managing these private screenings, stated that the production team wanted to avoid [self-censorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-censorship "Self-censorship") regarding content and therefore adopted an approach to screen the film globally by contacting various distributors to host single-time private screenings.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-PArticlesMarch2023-3) Filmmaker [Geling Yan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geling_Yan "Geling Yan"), while discussing [film censorship in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_censorship_in_China "Film censorship in China"), cited _A New Old Play_ as an example of the growing discontent among filmmakers regarding censorship, and referred to its unauthorised screenings as an alternative approach to filmmaking, distinct from simply shifting production outside the country.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-58)

_A New Old Play_'s critical reception was positive,[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-59) with _[Liberty Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_Times "Liberty Times")_ referring to it as "critically acclaimed".[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-60) On the [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), [100%](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_films_with_a_100%25_rating_on_Rotten_Tomatoes "List of films with a 100% rating on Rotten Tomatoes") of 9 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 8.5/10.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-61) As of August 2022, the film held a rating of 9.0/10 on the Chinese media review platform [Douban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douban "Douban"),[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-62) for which the _[International Examiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Examiner "International Examiner")_ described the score as "well received".[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-InternationalExaminerSeptember2022-51)

Austin Considine of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_ described _A New Old Play_ as a "magnificently layered historical epic", blending tragedy and farce with crafted [mise-en-scène](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mise-en-sc%C3%A8ne "Mise-en-scène"), while infusing humour into a narrative that grapples with the "absurdities and indignities" of life amidst the turmoil of Chinese history.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-NYTReview-1) _[Film Threat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_Threat "Film Threat")_'s Calan Panchoo rated the film 8.5/10, praising its "astonishing imagination" in combining art and history through a "salient" presentation achieved with "beautifully realized" production design, "wickedly puckish humor", and a "wonderful visual suggestion" that balances [realism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Realism_/(arts/) "Realism (arts)") and [surrealism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrealism "Surrealism"), resulting in a "multilayered" exploration of history and memory in contemporary Chinese history.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-FilmThreatReview-63)

[Richard Brody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Brody "Richard Brody") at _[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Yorker "The New Yorker")_ found the story to be a "daringly and imaginatively" dramatised account of 20th-century Chinese political history, presenting a highly personal and intimate portrayal of a small theatre company amid ongoing [film censorship in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_censorship_in_China "Film censorship in China"), employing theatrical techniques and "archly" ironic elements to emphasise the narrative's complexities.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-NewYorkerReview-2) Marta Bałaga, writing for _[Cineuropa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cineuropa "Cineuropa")_, called the film an "extraordinary" epic saga that, despite its "demanding" narrative richness and complex themes, remains a "pleasure, frequently humorous and always tender" exploration of the Sichuan opera performers' lives amidst China's political turmoil, showcasing director Qiu Jiongjiong's deep affection for the art form.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-64) Stéphane Gobbo of _[Le Temps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Temps "Le Temps")_ also acknowledged the film's "wonderful homage" to traditional Chinese theatre and early cinema through its production design, noting that it effectively addresses historical themes with a unique and immersive narrative style.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-65)

_[InReview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/InReview "InReview")_'s Ryan Swen regarded the film as a "rich and complex contribution to the Chinese folk tradition", comparing it to _[The Travelling Players](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Travelling_Players "The Travelling Players")_ (1975) and _[Platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platform_/(2000_film/) "Platform (2000 film)")_ (2000) for their shared use of theatrical performances to depict history, while lauding its bold blend of theatricality and stylisation that creates an "intimate and aggregative" portrait of a [clown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chou_role "Chou role")'s journey through 20th-century history, ultimately celebrating the artistry of theatre amidst the inevitability of historical change and uncertainties.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-66) Wang Xia, on the other hand, noted similarities between the film and the works of [Roy Andersson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Andersson "Roy Andersson") in her review for _[China Film News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Film_News "China Film News")_, commending the "decent" and surrealistic production designs that connect to paintings, poetry, and theatre, while acknowledging the use of traditional theatrical performance's fictional elements to explore over half a century of Chinese history, "ingeniously balancing the absurd and the profound" in its reflection on themes of dignity, humour, and the interconnectedness of life and death.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_New_Old_Play#cite_note-ChinaFilmNewsReview-24)

_A New Old Play_ — Qiu Jiongjiong
=================================

[May 20, 2022](https://inreviewonline.com/2022/05/20/a-new-old-play-qiu-jiongjiong/) [\- by Ryan Swen](https://inreviewonline.com/the-writers/ryan-swen/)

![Image 3: A New Old Play film still. Man smoking, wearing a red cap. Face sculpture on wall. Qiu Jiongjiong film.](https://inreviewonline.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/A-NEW-OLD-PLAY-01_Courtesy-of-the-dGenerate-Collection-at-Icarus-Films-1024x579.jpg)

Credit: the dGenerate Collection at Icarus Films

_A New Old Play_ is a rich, complex contribution to the Chinese folk tradition, and a “theater” film for the ages.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

* * *

Without getting too far into Bresson’s dissection of the irreconcilable differences between the artistic media of film and theater, there has been a longstanding interest, and thus conundrum, in how to depict the staging of a theatrical production on film. From Busby Berkeley backstage musicals to _The Golden Coach_ to Rivette’s masterpieces to _Vanya on 42nd Street_ to, of course, _Drive My Car_, films about theater are typically just as much about the communal nature of the endeavor, the relationships that are formed in the intimate times of living and working together.

And then, there are those films, like _The Travelling Players_ and _Platform_, that use theater and performance as a means to convey and explore the grand sweep of history, as the relatively static nature of performance and style is met by larger social and governmental forces over decades. Qiu Jiongjiong’s feature debut, _A New Old Play_, fits in very much with this lineage of acting-troupe epics, running just under three hours and spanning the 1920s to the 1980s in the Sichuan Province. Unlike its predecessors, however, it totally focuses on a single actor: a clown, Qiufu, who is based on Qiu’s own grandfather. It also explicitly takes a retrospective look: the film begins with two demons arriving to bring him to hell, and the rest of the film threads this long journey alongside a chronological retelling of his ascent to stardom in the New-New Troupe and Opera School (at age seven), and how he, his family, and his collaborators weathered World War II, the Chinese Civil War, and the upheaval that the Chinese Communist Party introduced into an already fraught environment.

In a sharp break from the documentaries that have made up Qiu’s work to date, _A New Old Play_ instead opts for an approach that emphasizes artificiality and stylization of these spaces of the past and the supernatural. Seemingly every scene takes place on a set, each crafted to maximize what feels like a handcrafted quality to the film, where the distressed and flat personality permeates the backdrops of man-made structures and landscapes alike. A golden statue is embodied by living flesh, ocean currents by billowing fabric, and brick walls look like plywood painstakingly painted to suggest the mortar without fully defining it. All of these might strike one as budgetary necessities, but the effect here is far from, say, the nightmarish distortions of _The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari_ or the opposite approach of reflection of present onto past in _Platform_. Instead, this abstraction suggests an archetypal base to build upon, a physical closeness of space and a continuity between the “real world” and the purposeful unreality of theater, literalized in a shot that tracks right as bricks are rolled on-stage from a daytime view of distant mountains, then off-stage into the painted night sky and distant city. And while Qiu is free to mix up his style, throwing in oblique angles and handheld when necessary, much of the film is shot in single-direction tracking shots and tableaux teeming with people, where the distinctiveness of the faces meld into a tapestry of expressions and reactions, all similar but none totally alike.

That quality serves the film well: Qiufu is certainly the main character, set apart by this supernatural intervention and his obdurate commitment to craft, even as his fellow cast and crew fall away due to the ravages of time, while also being instantly recognizable thanks to his ever-present large ears, red nose, and beanie. But this is as much a portrait of community, leaving plenty of time to consider how people contend with the weight of change and history, each interaction another building block in a conception of history that is resolutely intimate and aggregative. Even the intertitles that help clarify when the next decade has passed for those very unfamiliar with Chinese history — as someone of Chinese descent, the careful but never overstated intertwining of history into the narrative moved me — convey these changes in more poetic terms.

All this while, Qiufu is on his way to the afterlife, where he will have to drink a soup of forgetfulness to enter, or otherwise wander as a ghost among the living. This voyage into the unknown carries the same genial tone as _A New Old Play_, of a resigned acceptance of the inevitable that carries with it a whole world of mystery and discovery. The film closes with Qiu himself appearing in front of the camera, one of the most fitting cameos in ages, as he implicitly puts himself in the lineage of these performers and artists who have contributed to a rich Chinese folk tradition. On the strength of _A New Old Play_, such a gesture is more than earned.

[Home](https://thefilmverdict.com/) - [Festivals](https://thefilmverdict.com/category/festivals/) - A New Old Play

VERDICT: Director Qiu Jiongjiong uses a traditional theater troupe to spin out three long hours of dreamy reflections on Chinese history in the 20th century.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Filmmaker Qiu Jiongjiong’s grandfather achieved fame as a clown actor performing with a traditional Sichuan opera troupe, and in _A New Old Play_, the director’s first narrative feature, his grandfather’s life inspires a picaresque series of stories that traverse the tumultuous 20th century. Often entertaining, occasionally mesmerizing, but too often unnecessarily drawn out and ennui-inducing, the stories trace the violent course of Chinese history from the 1920s to Chiang Kai-shek’s reunification of China, followed by the ascent to power of Chairman Mao and the Communist Party. For aficionados and festivals, it remains a uniquely refined first film that shows the clash of political and social change with immutable traditions. But its 3-hour running time, theatrical stylization and leisurely pace will make it hard going for many viewers.

Bowing in Locarno’s main competition, the tales are loosely stitched together around the imminent death of the main character. In a recurrent scene, Qiu Fu (Yi Sicheng) appears as an old man whose time has come to go to the City of Ghosts. Two minions appear to accompany him on his last journey, where the King of Hell awaits him. His clever efforts to slip away are useless, and he stops in a country inn where he will drink the soup of oblivion and forget the life he has just led. In this intriguing space between life and death, he relives his long and difficult career.

His father was an actor who died on stage; his poverty-stricken mother took his little brother and abandoned Qiu Fu. A scrappy young boy, he is reluctantly taken in by the New-New Theater Troupe, which is run with army-like discipline and beatings by former general Pocky Liu. Among the colorful characters is old Master Crooky, who tenderly carries around the Holy Bodhisattva, a life-sized statue glowing with peace and wisdom (most unsettlingly, the statue is played by a person.)

After passing his fleas to everybody in the troupe, the boy embarks on his predestined acting career. But rather than the usual star-is-born saga, Qiu Jiongjiong chooses to craft an atmospheric mood piece around the entire troupe, who initially appear like ghosts on mainly white sets, designed and painted in expressly built Sichuan studios by the director himself. The results are original and often amazing, like the silhouettes of soldiers against the painted gates of a walled city, which will shortly by destroyed in a fury of bombardments, smoke and war.

The theme of war and death is omnipresent. In the 1930s, Pocky fought in the long war against the Japanese, until Japan was defeated in 1945. He was on the side of Nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek, but retired when the communist Mao Zedong founded the People’s Republic of China.

At this point the New-New troupe disbands. Qiu Fu and his young wife, an actress, spend their days getting stoned on opium. Many of the actors sail to Taiwan on a boat that could have come out of Fellini’s _And the Ship Sails On_. But when Qiu, his wife and small daughter get to Taiwan, they discover no one is interested in Chinese arias or clown comedy, and they become beggars.

As the red flag is unfurled over northern China introducing a new society and a new era, Pocky brings his actors home. The troupe is optimistically re-dubbed “Joyful Theater” and “People’s Theater”; but it’s a pretense. Soon they will be reviled as counter-revolutionaries and made to wear dunce caps and signs around their necks. Though the great traditions of Chinese opera seem to have been buried forever, there is still old Crooky carrying around the Holy Bodhisattva, hiding his glowing light under a burlap sack.

The grueling poverty of those days is brought home in some of the film’s most unforgettable scenes, involving a newborn baby that Qiu Fu brings home to his wife (Guan Nan) shortly after their own daughter has died of starvation. First the wife resists “another mouth to feed”, but when the baby is near death, the couple steals into a fog-shrouded area to pick maggots (“an excellent source of protein”) out of human excrement, only to be told that both the excrement and maggots belong to the state.

The fictional backdrop is beautifully served by Robbin Fen’s evocative cinematography, which seems inspired by cloudy opium dreams of a past time that can be vaguely remembered but never recovered. In many ways, the film is a reimagining of Qiu Jiongjiong’s feature documentary _Mr. Zhang Believes (_Locarno 2015), which also tapped theater and autobiography to recount 20th century Chinese history in a highly personal authorial voice.

_Director, screenwriter, production design, editing: Qiu Jiongjiong  
Cast: Yi Sicheng, Guan Nan, Qiu Zhimin, Xue Xuchun, Gu Tao  
__Producers: Ding Ding, Yang Jin  
__Executive producers: L. Sophie, Han Yi, Huang Yue, Bao Vivian, Tang Xastle, Su Qiqi  
__Director of photography: Robbin Feng  
__Costume design: Bai Yun  
__Music: Diao Lili  
__Sound: Wang Ran  
__Production companies: Uluka Productions (Hong Kong), Hippocampe Productions (France) in association with Midnight Blur (China)  
__World sales: Parallax Films  
__Venue: Locarno Film Festival (international competition)__  
179 minutes_

QIU Jiongjiong’s visually magnificent new film is a unique hybrid of fiction, historical reminiscence, and experimental theatre. Its overview of China from the 1930s to the 1980s is filtered through Qiu Yu, a Sichuan opera 'clown' based on the director’s own famous grandfather. As Qiu Yu negotiates his entry into Hades with two comic sidekicks, his departing soul reviews his childhood, his performances, family tragedies, and political perils.

This film of unparalleled aesthetic and political courage takes place in modestly spectacular visual settings: Qiu, a famous artist, has handcrafted an exquisite miniature model village, a fantastical river landscape, a golden sun in the shape of a Buddha’s head. These images set the scene for a constantly shifting acting style that embraces absurdism, political melodrama, comic vaudeville, and ritual tableaux. We are offered memory as a re-lived collective experience, insistently comic in its mode, but expansively humane in its vision. —IFFR

_“Critic’s Pick! A magnificently layered historical epic... breathes new life into a story as old as civilization.”_ **—Austin Considine, The New York Times**

_“Director Qiu creates a huge epochal fresco and revives the ancient Sichuan Opera tradition with the magic touch of a modern-day Méliès.”_ **—Maria Giovanna Vagenas, Senses of Cinema**

_“Daring and imaginative, with affecting intimacy and candid observations.”_ **—Richard Brody, The New Yorker**

_“An epic and fantastical depiction of five decades of Chinese history.”_ **—Richard Whittaker, The Austin Chronicle**

_“The brightest light in the Chinese independent cinema world at this moment.”_ **—Cinema Scope**

![Image 1: Flicks with The Film Snob](https://kxci.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/Untitled-Artwork-4-220x220.jpg)

Flicks with The Film Snob

A New Old Play

![Image 2: Loading](https://kxci.org/wp-content/plugins/seriously-simple-podcasting/assets/css/images/player/images/icon-loader.svg)

![Image 3](https://kxci.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/newoldplay.jpg)**  
The fictional account of a Chinese opera troupe covers, in epic and satiric style, the course of Chinese history from the 1920s through the 1970s.**

A friend once teased me, calling me “the boy who cried masterpiece,” because of my over-fondness for that word. But I’m going to use that word again, having recently watched the latest film from Chinese director Qiu Jiongjiong, called **_A New Old Play_**. It’s a stunning 3-hour epic drama, with satirical elements, about a fictional Chinese opera troupe, from the 1920s through the early 1970s.

We start with a strange framing device. Two figures emerge from behind a hill, one of them making a sound like a horse, the other like an ox, and pedaling a raggedy looking carriage decked with lights. They are ancient messengers from the underworld, the land of the dead, and they’re here to transport a well-known opera performer named Qiu Fu, and played by Yi Sicheng, to the afterlife after his recent death. Qiu tries to argue with the spirits, but in the end he has no choice. He has to travel with them, first through a shadowy netherworld and eventually across a river to his final home. While wandering through the netherworld, he reminisces about his life and the history of his opera troupe in extended flashbacks which take up the bulk of the film.

The orphaned son of a famous actor, Qiu tags along with his father’s former Sichuan opera company in the 1920s. They laugh at him and try to kick him out, but the master of the troupe sees something in him, and he’s given training. This is an innovative group—China having recently become a republic—that seeks to modernize the art, with one of the key innovations being allowing women to play female characters. We follow Qiu’s story, as a youth, then a young man, to success as the company’s number one clown. There are also many other characters who are granted a point of view in the story: it’s a rich fabric of interesting relationships. Crucially, the personal stories are set against the dramatic stages of 20th century Chinese history.

The director, Qiu, has an eye for the telling detail. For this story, he employs theatrical devices to create a kind of magical realist effect. We feel the intense historical reality while recognizing the artificiality of the form. The sets are obviously painted sets, and the many props and other production details are clearly the kind you might see on a stage, but brought out to beautiful effect by the camera and its many tracking shots across the scenes that are presented for maximum effect. Almost every sequence, every shot in the movie contains something to stimulate, provoke, or puzzle the viewer. The historical reality is conveyed through the slightest means. When Mao takes over the country, the new training of the theater company to conform to party doctrine is darkly comical, as we can see its effect on the already jaded performers. The film’s title comes to mind here: _A New Old Play_. It’s like the lyric from that song by The Who: “Meet the new boss, same as the old boss.”

The film doesn’t flinch from recalling the tragedies of Chinese history. It covers the famine that killed millions in the ‘50s. It covers the so-called Cultural Revolution in the ‘60s, with its stupid scapegoating of an entire generation. We see a prisoner in one of the work camps building a brick enclosure that will eventually entrap him. But the symbolism goes even beyond politics. Those entering the underworld must first drink from a stream of forgetfulness. Forgetting is the ultimate price. But this film, this masterpiece, _A New Old Play,_ won’t let us forget.

* * *

The Chinese Cinema Project presents a mini-season celebrating Qiu Jiongjiong, showcasing his early non-fiction works and this modern classic.

[Middle East](https://streamlined.news/tag/middle-east/)A New Old Play was named best film in the Chinese section, while Mediterranean Fever took best film in the World section.

[![Image 1: Liz Shackleton](https://www.gravatar.com/avatar/d016d35ce5ce113cf602f587acb46e0a?s=250&r=x&d=mp)](https://streamlined.news/author/liz/)

![Image 2: A New Old Play](https://streamlined.news/content/images/size/w1200/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/a-new-old-play.jpg)

_****A New Old Play****_

**Chinese filmmaker Qiu Jiongjiong's A New Old Play was named best film in the Young Cinema Competition (Chinese-language) of the Firebird Awards at this year’s Hong Kong International Film Festival (HKIFF). Palestinian director Maha Haj's Mediterranean Fever won the same honours in the Young Cinema Competition (World) section of the awards.**

The jury hailed _A New Old Play_, the story of a family of Sichuan Opera artists living through a tumultuous era, as “one of this year's most distinguished films both creatively and artistically”. Besides winning the Firebird Award, the film also won the prize of the FIPRESCI jury, who commented on its “masterful approach and inventive visual style”.

Also in the Chinese-language competition, Hong Kong's Mak Pui-tung won best actor for _The Sparring Partner_, while best actress went to Ailiya for her performance in _Journey To The West_. The jury chose to not award a prize for best director.

In the Young Cinema Competition (World) section, _Mediterranean Fever_ was awarded for being “an all-rounded gem that is at once a thriller, social comedy, and odd couple bromance.”

French and Belgian co-production _Love According To Dalva_ picked up two prizes in this section – best director went to Emmanuelle Nicot and best actress to Zelda Samson. The best actor award went to Moritz Treuenfels for playing a pathological liar in _Axiom_.

The jury for the Young Cinema Competition (Chinese-language) section included producer Nai An and filmmakers Peter Ho-sun Chan and Anthony Chen. The jury for the Young Cinema Competition (World) section comprised producer and festival consultant Raymond Phathanavirangoon, Iranian actor and director Niki Karimi and Hong Kong distributor and critic Fred Tsui.

In the Documentary Competition, the jury unanimously gave the Firebird Award to Indian filmmaker Shaunak Sen's _All That Breathes_, while Vietnamese director Ha Le Diem received the Jury Prize for _Children Of The Mist_.

Chilean filmmakers were the big winners in the Short Film Competition with Hugo Covarrubias’ _Bestia_ selected as the Firebird Award winner for its distinctive animation aesthetics, while Cristóbal León and Joaquín Cociña collected the Jury Prize for _The Bones_. Brazilian director Carlos Segundo’s _Sideral_ received a Special Mention.

HKIFF ran from August 15-31 after being postponed from its usual April slot due to the Covid-19 pandemic. The festival screened more than 200 films from 67 countries and regions, including 32 Asian and four world premieres across 17 days of in-theatre and online screenings. Next year’s edition of the festival has been scheduled for March 30-April 10, 2023.

Critic’s Pick

Qiu Jiongjiong’s absurdist epic of 20th century China is both a movie and a play, both tragedy and farce.

![Image 1](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2022/05/20/arts/newold1/merlin_206732253_666201fe-a3e2-4af3-b6ff-f2c682dab035-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&disable=upscale)

Yi Sicheng in “A New Old Play.”Credit...Icarus Films

May 19, 2022

A New Old Play

NYT Critic’s Pick

Directed by Qiu Jiongjiong

Biography, History

2h 59m

Per the title, Qiu Jiongjiong’s magnificently layered historical epic, “A New Old Play,” draws as much from Brecht and Beckett as from cinematic traditions. At once tragedy and farce, it breathes new life into a story as old as civilization.

The opening scene is disorienting at first, not least for the film’s protagonist, Qiu Fu (Yi Sicheng), a well-known actor from a Sichuan opera troupe. We meet him when he is old and stooping, in a crumbling mountain village enshrouded by fog. It is China in the 1980s, and the Japanese, the nationalists and the communists have wreaked their havoc in turn. Now two raggedy demons have arrived in a broken-down bicycle rickshaw to cart Qiu off to the underworld.

Still, something feels uncanny, demons notwithstanding. The entire mise-en-scène of the film, we discover, is artificial, an assembly of stage props and hand-painted scenery. Qiu has always played the clown, shuffling from scene to scene, a hapless pauper harassed by need and political fashion. Even his wife (Guan Nan) may not miss him when he’s gone. Somehow he, like the film, maintains a sense of humor. Such is life for a poor player.

Qiu isn’t keen to leave, but his time is up — as the demons remind him, it’s no use trying to outrun fate. Also, the King of Hell is a fan, and Qiu’s failure to appear would make them look bad.

But first, let’s drink and play mahjong in purgatory, where Qiu awaits final passage to oblivion. Absurdities and indignities mount as he reminisces about a life spanning wars and famine, revolution and betrayal. The director’s cleverest trick is having also found joy there.

**A New Old Play**  
Not rated. In Mandarin, with subtitles. Running time: 2 hours 59 minutes. In theaters.
